seen.where: Browne's typeset reproduction of the signs in E. G. Browne, 'Catalogue and Description of 27 Babi Manuscripts', JRAS 1892: p. 489 (BBF. 4 = F. 43, end of the Naghamat al-ruh, f. 101b) and p. 651 (BBF. 9 = F. 16, colophon, f. 261a), read on the archive.org scan of JRAS n.s. 24 (item journalofroyalas2418roya, leaves n510 and n672, page images 1537 x 2683 px, the digit line cropped and enlarged). The manuscripts themselves were not seen: no CUDL record found (cudl.lib.cam.ac.uk/iiif/MS-BROWNE-F-00043 answers 500 where a known item answers 200; images.lib.cam.ac.uk IIIF ids MS-BROWNE-F-00043/-00016 404), and the Fihrist records say 'Contact near_eastern@lib.cam.ac.uk for further information on the availability of this manuscript'.
seen.extent: Very short. F. 43: two groups of Eastern Arabic (Persian-form) digits under the explicit, printed as 5331685 and 3125311376 (7 + 10 digits); Browne says the same cyphers are repeated at the end of the La'ali u Majali (F. 43 f. 203a) and at the end of BBF. 5 (= F. 39, Subh-i Azal's Persian writings), which were not printed again. F. 16: five digits ending the colophon after 'he who needeth the grace of his Bountiful Lord', printed in Persian digits and rendered by Browne as 51092. About 22 digits in all.
seen.cipher: Numeral cypher standing for a name: Browne, p. 489: the cyphers 'indicate, as Subh-i-Ezel informed me by word of mouth, that the writings to which they are appended are by him. Their significance, however, he was not willing to divulge to me' (Browne then guesses at the abjad notation); p. 651 n. 1: 'The cyphers at the end of the colophon appear to represent in some cabbalistic fashion the scribe's name.' Browne prints the digits with no reading, and says none was given to him; nothing of a decipherment is printed with them.

prior_art.edition: Browne's own JRAS 1892 catalogue (pp. 489, 651) is the edition: it prints the digits and leaves them unexplained. Nicholson's Descriptive Catalogue of the Oriental MSS belonging to the late E. G. Browne (1932; archive.org b31361596, full text searched) describes F. 43 and F. 16 only by reference to Browne 1892 and has no mention of cyphers. The Fihrist records repeat Browne.
prior_art.literature: Web searches on Subh-i Azal's numerical signature, abjad, colophon cyphers and MacEoin's Sources for Early Babi Doctrine and History found nothing explaining these digits; the nearest material is the documented Baha'i convention of signing with 152 / 251 (= b-h-a, Baha) and Browne's note that Yahya equals Wahid in abjad, neither of which is a reading of these groups.

2895.key_check: No key in the manuscripts is recorded by Browne or Nicholson. The obvious first test, not made here (vetting does not attempt a reading): the Babi/Baha'i convention printed by Browne in the same JRAS volume, p. 273, where Baron Rosen reads Baha'u'llah's cypher 152 as the letters alif, ha, ba = Baha (digits as abjad letter values), and Browne's own guess that Azal's cyphers 'refer in some way to the abjad notation'.
2895.key_held: Rosen's digit-as-abjad-letter reading of the 152 (Baha) cypher, JRAS 1892 p. 273; a convention of the same milieu, not a key shown to read these groups; not tested.

2896.unvetted: Prior art not settled: Verena Klemm, 'A Library in One Volume - The Notebook of the Nineteenth-Century Isma'ili Scholar Sayyidi Muhammad 'Ali al-Hamdani from Surat', Die Welt des Islams 65/4 (2025) 381-414, open access, is a study of IIS MS 1662 itself and was not opened (brill.com 403 to scripts; Klemm's blog post on globalcommentary.utoronto.ca sits behind a JavaScript bot check, not passed). Ciphertext not seen: the IIS record says 'No image available for this record'. The IIS online entry (de Blois 2011) does show cipher survives on fol. 83b ('Notes written in the same system of cipher that Muhammad 'Ali used in Ms. 1499') and fols 29a-b ('much of it in cipher') and gives no reading. Next: read Klemm 2025 in a browser for fols 29a-b and 83b, then ask the IIS for images.
